speakerBio: Acute physician and patient-safety lead who reviews every DKA and HHS incident in the trust and teaches that in hyperglycaemic emergencies the treatment is often more dangerous than the disease.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 12-year-old is admitted in DKA — pH 7.02, glucose 29, drowsy but rousable. The team runs a textbook resuscitation: generous fluid boluses, fixed-rate insulin, and the numbers improve beautifully. Four hours in, the biochemistry looks great — glucose 12, pH 7.28 — and everyone relaxes. Then the child complains of a headache, becomes irritable, then suddenly less responsive; the heart rate drops from 120 to 60 and the blood pressure climbs. The improving numbers hid a deteriorating brain: this is cerebral oedema, and the very treatment that fixed the biochemistry caused it. This session is about the uncomfortable truth of hyperglycaemic emergencies — that many of the ways these patients are harmed are iatrogenic, caused by us, and are therefore preventable if you know where to look.

1 · 🧠 Cerebral oedema — the feared iatrogenic catastrophe

Cerebral oedema is the most dreaded complication of DKA treatment, and it is overwhelmingly a disease of children and young people — rare in adults. It is uncommon (roughly 0.5–1% of paediatric DKA) but carries a mortality of 20–25% and leaves many survivors with permanent neurological injury.

The mechanism

  1. During DKA the brain adapts to hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality by accumulating intracellular idiogenic osmoles to protect its water content.
  2. When treatment lowers glucose and plasma osmolality too rapidly, the plasma becomes relatively hypotonic to the brain.
  3. Water follows the osmotic gradient into brain cells — cytotoxic and vasogenic oedema — and the rigid skull leaves no room, so intracranial pressure rises.

Contributing factors implicated in studies include a high initial urea (marker of dehydration severity), a low initial pCO₂, treatment with bicarbonate, aggressive early fluid volumes, and giving insulin within the first hour.

Warning signs — recognise them early

  • Headache and recurrence of, or new, irritability/agitation.
  • Falling conscious level (GCS drop) — the most important sign.
  • The Cushing response: bradycardia + rising blood pressure (± irregular respiration) — a late and ominous sign of raised ICP.
  • Cranial nerve palsies, abnormal posturing, incontinence, falling oxygen saturations.
⚠️ Treat on suspicion — do not wait for the scan

If cerebral oedema is suspected clinically, treat immediately — do not delay for CT confirmation. Give hypertonic saline (2.7–3%) or mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg), slow the intravenous fluids, nurse head-up, call ICU/paediatric intensive care and a senior. A normal early CT does not exclude it. The scan is to look for other pathology, not to grant permission to treat.

In a child whose DKA numbers are improving but whose brain is deteriorating, assume cerebral oedema and treat it before the CT.

2 · 🩸 Treatment hypokalaemia — the commonest killer

Covered in depth in the potassium session, but it belongs at the top of any pitfalls list because it is the commonest preventable cause of death in DKA. Insulin drives potassium into cells; the total-body store is already depleted; serum potassium therefore falls fast once treatment starts. The errors are: not checking potassium before insulin, starting insulin when K⁺ < 3.5, and failing to add 40 mmol/L KCl to the fluids once K⁺ is in the 3.5–5.5 band.

💡 One line to remember

Every DKA death review that finds a flat T wave and a U wave on the monitor traces back to the same root cause: insulin was given faster than potassium was replaced. Check K⁺ before insulin, replace at 40 mmol/L for the middle band, monitor the heart.

3 · 📉 Hypoglycaemia — forgetting the dextrose

In DKA the insulin infusion is fixed-rate and must keep running to clear the ketones — you cannot simply turn it off when the glucose normalises, or ketogenesis restarts. The pitfall is failing to add glucose to the fluids when the blood glucose falls, producing iatrogenic hypoglycaemia while the insulin runs on.

  • The rule: once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, start 10% glucose infusion (typically 125 mL/h) alongside the saline, and continue the fixed-rate insulin.
  • The insulin is switched off only when the DKA has resolved (ketones < 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH > 7.3 / bicarbonate > 15) and the patient is eating with subcutaneous insulin restarted — not simply when the glucose is normal.
  • Hypoglycaemia is dangerous in its own right and also triggers counter-regulatory hormones that can worsen ketosis — a double hit.
Glucose below 14 means add dextrose, not stop insulin. The insulin clears the ketones; the dextrose stops the hypo.

4 · 🌊 Fluid overload & pulmonary oedema

The mirror image of under-resuscitation. Aggressive fluid regimens designed for a young, fit type 1 patient can drown an elderly patient with cardiac or renal impairment. HHS patients — old, comorbid — are especially vulnerable, which is one reason their fluids are given more slowly.

  • Watch for pulmonary oedema (breathlessness, hypoxia, crepitations, rising oxygen requirement) and fluid overload in anyone elderly, or with heart failure or CKD.
  • Tailor the rate: use more cautious fluid regimens, consider closer haemodynamic monitoring, and involve seniors early in the frail patient.
  • Excessive rapid fluid in children is also implicated in cerebral oedema — the caution cuts both ways across the age spectrum.

5 · 🧂 Hyperchloraemic acidosis — the benign impostor

A patient several hours into DKA treatment can have a persisting low bicarbonate and a normal anion gap — the ketones have cleared but the acidosis has not fully resolved. Before you panic and escalate treatment, recognise this for what it usually is: a hyperchloraemic (normal-anion-gap) metabolic acidosis from the large volumes of 0.9% saline (chloride 154 mmol/L) infused during resuscitation.

  • It is a consequence of treatment, is usually benign, and resolves spontaneously over 24–48 hours as the kidney handles the chloride load.
  • The key is to track ketones and the anion gap, not the bicarbonate alone. If ketones are < 0.6 and the anion gap has normalised, the residual acidosis is hyperchloraemic and needs no specific action.
  • Misreading it as ongoing DKA leads to inappropriate continuation of high-rate insulin and risks hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia.
💡 Follow the ketones, not the bicarbonate

DKA resolution is defined by ketones < 0.6 mmol/L and a closed anion gap, not by a normal bicarbonate. A lingering low bicarbonate with cleared ketones is hyperchloraemic acidosis from saline — benign, self-limiting, no action needed.

6 · 🔄 Rebound ketoacidosis — stopping insulin too soon

A classic and entirely preventable readmission. If the intravenous insulin is stopped before the patient has overlapping subcutaneous insulin on board — or is stopped just because the glucose looks normal — endogenous insulin is still absent, ketogenesis restarts within an hour or two, and the patient rebounds straight back into DKA.

  • Never stop the IV insulin until DKA has resolved (ketones < 0.6, pH > 7.3) and the patient is eating.
  • Give the first dose of subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin with a meal and overlap it with the IV infusion for 30–60 minutes before stopping the drip — the overlap is essential because IV insulin has a half-life of only minutes.
  • Patients on long-acting basal insulin at home should ideally have it continued throughout the DKA episode, which smooths the transition and prevents rebound.
Never let the IV insulin stop before the subcutaneous insulin starts — the gap is where rebound DKA is born.

7 · 🤢 Aspiration & gastroparesis

DKA causes gastric stasis, and patients are often nauseated, vomiting and drowsy. The drowsy, vomiting DKA patient is at real risk of aspiration pneumonitis.

  • Consider a nasogastric tube in the patient with reduced consciousness and vomiting/gastric distension to decompress the stomach and reduce aspiration risk.
  • Nurse appropriately, protect the airway, and have a low threshold for anaesthetic/ICU input in the obtunded patient.

8 · 🔍 The missed precipitant

A pitfall of omission rather than commission: treating the metabolic derangement flawlessly while failing to find and treat what tipped the patient into it — the infection, the myocardial infarction, the missed insulin, the new steroids. The metabolic emergency can be perfectly corrected and the patient still deteriorate or die from an untreated precipitant. (This is the subject of the next session, but it belongs on every pitfalls list.)

10 · 💀 M&M — paediatric cerebral oedema

⚠️ Morbidity & Mortality: "the numbers looked perfect"

A 9-year-old girl presented in severe DKA (pH 6.98, glucose 33, markedly raised urea reflecting profound dehydration). Keen to correct her quickly, the team gave repeated large fluid boluses, started insulin within the first hour, and — troubled by the low pH — gave a dose of sodium bicarbonate. The biochemistry improved rapidly. Five hours in, with a glucose of 11 and a near-normal pH, she developed a headache and became difficult to rouse; her heart rate fell to 55 with a rising blood pressure. This was cerebral oedema. There was a delay while a CT was arranged "to confirm" before treatment; by the time mannitol was given she had fixed dilated pupils, and she died. The review identified a cluster of recognised risk factors, all modifiable: excessive early fluid, insulin within the first hour, bicarbonate administration, and a high presenting urea — compounded by the fatal decision to wait for imaging rather than treat on clinical suspicion. Correct DKA in a child gradually, avoid bicarbonate and early aggressive fluids, and if cerebral oedema is suspected, treat first and scan later.

11 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Many harms in hyperglycaemic emergencies are iatrogenic — caused by treatment and therefore preventable.
  2. Cerebral oedema is the feared complication of children/young people: caused by too-rapid falls in glucose/osmolality; warning signs are headache, GCS drop and bradycardia + hypertension; treat on suspicion with hypertonic saline/mannitol and slower fluids — do not wait for CT.
  3. Treatment hypokalaemia is the commonest killer — check K⁺ before insulin, replace at 40 mmol/L, monitor the heart.
  4. Add 10% glucose when glucose < 14 and keep the insulin running — do not create a hypo.
  5. Fluid overload/pulmonary oedema threatens the elderly, cardiac and renal patient — individualise fluids.
  6. Hyperchloraemic acidosis from saline is benign and self-limiting — follow ketones and the anion gap, not bicarbonate.
  7. Rebound ketoacidosis comes from stopping IV insulin before SC insulin is on board — overlap and continue basal.
  8. Protect the drowsy, vomiting patient from aspiration (consider NG tube).
  9. Always find and treat the precipitant.

moderatorQs.q: A 13-year-old whose DKA biochemistry is improving develops a headache, a falling GCS and a heart rate that has dropped from 120 to 58 with rising blood pressure. What is happening and what do you do — and what do you NOT do first?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: This is cerebral oedema until proven otherwise — the classic scenario of a child whose numbers improve while the brain deteriorates, with the ominous combination of headache, dropping conscious level and a Cushing response (bradycardia + hypertension) signalling raised intracranial pressure. You treat immediately: give hypertonic saline (2.7–3%) or mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg), slow the IV fluids, nurse head-up, and call paediatric intensive care and a senior urgently. What you must NOT do is wait for a CT scan to confirm the diagnosis before treating — the delay costs lives, a normal early scan does not exclude it, and imaging is to exclude other pathology, not to grant permission to treat. The mechanism is a too-rapid fall in glucose and osmolality drawing water into a brain that had adapted with idiogenic osmoles.

moderatorQs.q: Several hours into DKA treatment the ketones are 0.4 and the anion gap has normalised, but the bicarbonate is still 16 and the patient is mildly acidotic. Should you intensify treatment?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No. This is almost certainly hyperchloraemic (normal-anion-gap) metabolic acidosis caused by the large volumes of 0.9% saline (chloride 154 mmol/L) given during resuscitation — a benign, self-limiting consequence of treatment that resolves over 24–48 hours as the kidney clears the chloride. The critical point is that DKA resolution is defined by ketones < 0.6 mmol/L and a closed anion gap, not by a normal bicarbonate. Since the ketones have cleared and the gap is closed, the DKA has resolved; the residual low bicarbonate needs no specific action. Intensifying or prolonging high-rate insulin here would be a mistake, risking iatrogenic hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. Follow the ketones and the gap, not the bicarbonate.

moderatorQs.q: The glucose in your DKA patient has fallen to 12 mmol/L. A junior wants to switch off the insulin infusion. Why is that wrong, and what is the correct action?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Switching off the insulin here would be a serious error that risks rebound ketoacidosis. The fixed-rate insulin is not there to control the glucose — it is there to switch off ketogenesis and clear the ketones; stop it and, with no endogenous insulin, ketone production restarts within an hour or two. The correct action is to keep the insulin running and add intravenous 10% glucose (typically 125 mL/h) now that the glucose is below 14 mmol/L, which prevents hypoglycaemia while the insulin finishes clearing the ketones. The insulin is only stopped once the DKA has resolved (ketones < 0.6, venous pH > 7.3 / bicarbonate > 15) and the patient is eating with subcutaneous insulin given and overlapped for 30–60 minutes before the drip comes down.

audienceQs.q: Which children with DKA are at highest risk of cerebral oedema, and how do I reduce that risk during treatment?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The highest-risk are younger children, those with new-onset diabetes, and those presenting most severely — a low pH, a high presenting urea (marking profound dehydration) and a low pCO₂ are all associated. Treatment factors that increase the risk are giving too much fluid too fast, administering insulin within the first hour, using bicarbonate, and letting glucose/osmolality fall too rapidly. To reduce risk: rehydrate in a controlled, measured way over the recommended period rather than with aggressive boluses, delay starting insulin until fluids are running (about an hour in), avoid bicarbonate, aim for a gentle glucose fall and add dextrose once it drops below 14, and monitor the neurological status closely. If cerebral oedema is suspected, treat immediately with hypertonic saline or mannitol and slow the fluids — do not wait for a scan.

audienceQs.q: How should the transition from the IV insulin infusion to subcutaneous insulin be handled to avoid the patient bouncing back into DKA?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The key is the overlap. Because intravenous insulin has a half-life of only a few minutes, the moment the drip stops the patient has essentially no insulin, so you must have subcutaneous insulin on board first. Only transition once the DKA has actually resolved (ketones < 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH > 7.3 / bicarbonate > 15) and the patient is eating. Give the first dose of subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin with a meal and continue the IV infusion for 30–60 minutes after it before stopping. Patients on a home long-acting basal insulin should have it continued throughout the whole episode, which greatly smooths the handover. Stopping the infusion on a normal glucose alone, with no SC insulin given, is the classic setup for rebound ketoacidosis and readmission.

audienceQs.q: My elderly HHS patient with heart failure is getting litres of saline and now sounds wet at the bases. What's going on and what do I do?
audienceQs.answerHTML: This is iatrogenic fluid overload with early pulmonary oedema — a real hazard when fluid regimens meant for young fit patients are applied to elderly, cardiac or renal patients, and HHS patients are especially vulnerable, which is exactly why their fluids are given more cautiously and slowly. Assess for breathlessness, hypoxia, raised JVP and basal crepitations, sit the patient up, give oxygen, slow or pause the infusion and reassess the fluid balance, and consider a diuretic if frankly overloaded. Escalate to a senior early and consider closer haemodynamic monitoring. Going forward, individualise the fluid rate to this patient's cardiac and renal reserve rather than following a generic high-rate regimen, while still correcting the large deficit gradually over 24–48 hours.
